title: The hypertrophy series: the inevitability of frequency control for optimal progression
summary: NH argues that frequency is as important as volume and intensity, the 'holy trinity' of programming, which can't be separated. For naturals it's the most neglected lever and the one left when volume and intensity stall. Spreading the same work across the week beats cramming it into one day, and legs and especially upper back respond to high frequency.
claims: Volume, intensity and frequency are inseparable, a 'holy trinity'; changing one changes the others
Claiming frequency doesn't matter for natural lifters shows a misunderstanding; the idea is mostly spread by steroid users, for whom frequency works differently
Because it is the most ignored variable, frequency is the most important one for natural lifters
If you hit a muscle only once a week, you're either sandbagging a muscle that's already strong or not progressing
There is a limit to daily volume (maximum recoverable volume) and intensity; when both stall, frequency is the lever left
Tonnage is king; it is the product of volume, intensity and frequency, and controlling them lets naturals keep progressing
A 3x3 squat on Monday, Wednesday and Friday beats doing all 9 sets on Monday, which would force lighter weights and cardio limits
Spreading sessions gives distance from training to assess gains; cramming all volume into one day only works for people on juice
For big legs naturally, train legs every two days; an upper/lower run six times a week gives three leg days
The upper back can be trained five times a week because it recovers quickly; try daily pull-ups or rows
A muscle that can't get meaningful volume within one session can often be trained fresh again after 24 hours
Ignoring frequency means also ignoring parameters of volume and intensity
Be wary of anyone who says an entire part of programming can be ignored: only intensity, only volume, or only frequency
